extracted.intended_audience: poets, critics, and educated readers evaluating heroic/epic poetry (readers of The Spectator)
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive critical guidance for the language and style of an heroic/epic poem (with extended examples drawn from Milton) and allied prescriptive norms for polite behaviour/writing in essays and letters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language of an heroic poem: perspicuous and sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: The language of an heroic poem should be both perspicuous and sublime; lack of either quality makes the language imperfect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perspicuity is primary — a reader must be able to grasp the poet's sense even if there are small grammatical slips. Sublimity requires deviation from ordinary expressions so the diction elevates thought without becoming stiff or unintelligible. Both qualities must be balanced: clarity first, then loftiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perspicuity (clarity) as the first qualification
rubrics_metrics.description: Perspicuity is the most necessary qualification; little slips in grammar or syntax may be pardoned when the thought is great and natural, because a good reader overlooks minor errors if the meaning is clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small syntactic ambiguities (examples from Milton where Divine Persons seem 'created' or Adam is confused with his children) are tolerable where overall sense and greatness of thought make meaning recoverable. Aim for clear expression even in elevated diction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublimity: elevated diction distinct from common speech
rubrics_metrics.description: To be sublime, a poem's diction must deviate from common forms and ordinary phrases of speech so as to avoid meanness and produce grandeur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid idiomatic or quotidian expressions that sound 'vulgar' in poetry. But avoid the 'false sublime' — affected grandiosity that hurts perspicuity. The poet must balance elevated expression with naturalness, steering between prosaic idiom and overblown affectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid idiomatic/common phrases that debase poetic dignity
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases used in ordinary conversation become too familiar and can make a poetical passage seem mean; great poets must guard against common idioms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not take the first, obvious phrase; seek expressions that are both natural and elevated. Examples: critics note Ovid and Lucan sometimes used the first phrases that offered and so produced 'poornesses of expression'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of metaphors (Aristotle's method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Metaphors are a principal method of raising language; they should be bold but just, sparingly used and not so dense as to clash with one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ striking, appropriate metaphors (many in Milton are cited) but avoid sowing metaphors 'so thick' that sentences become enigmas or riddles. Metaphors should enhance sense, not obscure it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of idioms/structures from other tongues (Hellenisms, Latinisms, Hebraisms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Infusing idioms and turns of speech from other languages raises the poetical tone and departs from the language of the vulgar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt foreign idiomatic turns (e.g., placing adjective after substantive, transpositions, turning adjectives into substantives) judiciously to give weight and novelty to diction. This practice should suit the genius of the language and be moderated by taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lengthening/contracting phrases and metrical manipulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Lengthening a phrase by addition, or contracting words and syllables (elisions), can elevate diction and vary verse measure; Milton uses such processes where English allows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use insertion/omission of words or syllables, and occasional elisions (e.g., variable treatment of final 'y') to diversify rhythm and avoid monotony in long blank verse. Apply these techniques with metrical awareness so they support, not ruin, the line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of old words and coinages to give antiquity and force
rubrics_metrics.description: Choosing venerable, archaic words and coining new terms can give a poem an air of antiquity and expand its expressive resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton's use of archaic words and coinages (e.g., Cerberean, miscreated) is defended: such liberties are allowable in poets (and Homer is cited as precedent). Still, the poet must ensure coinages are intelligible and contribute to, not obscure, meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation and judicious intermixture (avoid composing entirely of unusual words)
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive use of metaphors or foreign/unusual words produces either an enigma (if only metaphors) or a barbarous jargon (if only foreign words); moderation is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow Aristotle's counsel: intermix unusual and common words sensibly. A proper and temperate use of metaphors and foreign words heightens heroic diction; overuse makes verse obscure or ridiculous. Critics should prefer candour over captiousness when faults are minor among greater merits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pomp of sound and energy of expression required in blank verse
rubrics_metrics.description: Because blank verse lacks rhyme to distance itself from prose, it requires pomp of sound and energetic expression to keep from falling into prose-like flatness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing long narrative in blank verse, employ sonorous diction, varied rhythm, and elevated phrasing to sustain interest; rhyme alone can mask deficiencies that blank verse must expose and correct by stronger stylistic resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elisions and metric variety to prevent monotony in long narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Strategic elisions (suppression of syllables) and other metric innovations can vary numbers and prevent the ear from being satiated by uniform measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton's frequent elisions and measures that shorten syllables are examples; use such devices to introduce variety. But be attentive to audible read-throughs: if elision ruins the line when read, it is not justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: True delicacy in moral/polemical writing: truth and virtue as standards
rubrics_metrics.description: True delicacy consists in exactness of judgment and dignity of sentiment (purity of affection); the standard of delicacy is truth and virtue rather than squeamishness or affectation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not give fair names to foul actions — euphemizing vice confounds vice and virtue. In moral criticism and public writing, be severe where warranted (e.g., on deliberate pampered vice) and avoid treating grave sins as mere social foibles. The writer's aim should be public good and moral clarity, not smoothing or protecting vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity in letters and manners: avoid affected carelessness or perpetual hurry
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters and outward behaviour reveal true temper; affectations (professed careless unconcern or perpetual hurry) are follies that betray insincerity and poor taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In personal correspondence and social manners, avoid pretending not to think, or bragging of being 'too busy' — such postures indicate vanity and produce execution of nothing. Similarly, the affected 'careless' persona (e.g., claiming worst memory) or constant professions of being obliged elsewhere are criticized as social vices; write and behave authentically.
